final_answer: Antibiotic resistance arises through natural selection, a process where bacteria with genetic mutations conferring resistance to antibiotics survive and reproduce more than susceptible strains. When antibiotics are used, they kill most bacteria, but resistant mutants may persist. These survivors pass on their resistance genes to offspring, increasing their prevalence over generations. Overprescription accelerates this by applying frequent selective pressure, favoring resistant strains. Additionally, misuse (e.g., incomplete courses) allows partial killing, which may not eliminate all resistant bacteria, further promoting their spread. Horizontal gene transfer (e.g., plasmids) also spreads resistance genes between species, compounding the issue. Thus, overuse creates an environment where resistance evolves and disseminates rapidly.
